title: Egyptian Mythology: Figures, Relationships and Story Cycles
description: The Egyptian pantheon mapped as a relationship graph: the primordial waters, the Ennead of Heliopolis, the solar cycle, the Osiris myth, the powers of the Duat and the protective household gods.
sources: E. A. Wallis Budge, The Book of the Dead (1895), Legends of the Gods (1912), The Egyptian Heaven and Hell (1905) and The Gods of the Egyptians (1904)
W. M. Flinders Petrie, Egyptian Tales (1895)
Plutarch, Isis and Osiris, translated by William W. Goodwin (1874)
James Henry Breasted, Development of Religion and Thought in Ancient Egypt (1912)
Encyclopaedia Britannica and Wikipedia for cross-checking cult sites and periods
portraitNote: Portraits are original illustrations in a single uniform style for the whole pack, stored locally in the portraits/egyptian/ folder. No images are fetched from the network.

bod.t: The Book of the Dead (Papyrus of Ani)

breasted.t: Development of Religion and Thought in Ancient Egypt

profile.cosmicNature: Cyclical and continuously renewed, but always under threat. Each sunrise repeats the first sunrise, and each night the sun must pass through the underworld and survive an attack; the cosmos is not wound up once but re-won daily. Beyond that daily cycle stands zep tepi, the First Time, the perfect moment of creation that every ritual attempts to re-enter.
profile.natureOfDivinity: Fluid and combinatory. A god is a set of functions rather than a fixed person, so deities merge and separate without contradiction - Ra-Horakhty, Amun-Ra, Ptah-Sokar-Osiris - and the same god appears as falcon, as man, as falcon-headed man, or as a disc, depending on which aspect is meant. Local theologies at Heliopolis, Memphis and Hermopolis each claimed the creation for their own god without any felt need to reconcile.
profile.afterlife: An assessment, and then a continued existence requiring maintenance. The heart is weighed against the feather of Maat before forty-two judges; a heart heavier than truth is eaten by Ammit and the person ends entirely. Those who pass go on to the Field of Reeds, but the dead still need a preserved body, a spoken name and offerings, so the afterlife depends on the living keeping their side of it.
profile.systemMechanism: The maintenance of maat - truth, order, balance - against isfet, chaos. The king exists to uphold maat by ritual, the gods uphold it in the cosmos, and every individual is judged on it at death. The great enemy is not a rival god with a claim to the throne but Apep, the serpent of unbeing, who attacks the solar barque every night and must be repelled again every night.
profile.canonTexts: The Pyramid Texts, Coffin Texts and Book of the Dead, temple inscriptions at Edfu, Dendera and Abydos, the Memphite Theology of the Shabaka Stone, and the narrative papyri, with Plutarch's Isis and Osiris preserving the fullest connected account of the Osiris myth.

entities.name: Nun
entities.role: The primordial waters
symbols: upraised arms lifting the solar barque
entities.abode: Everywhere outside the created world, and still beneath it
entities.bio: The dark, limitless, motionless water that existed before anything else, and still surrounds the world.
entities.longBio: Nun is not a creator and does not act; he is the condition that preceded action. Egyptian cosmology begins with an infinite dark water without surface or current, and creation happens when a mound of earth rises out of it and the first god stands on that mound. Crucially, Nun is not destroyed by this. He remains outside the created order and beneath it, so that every well and every inundation of the Nile touches him, and the world is understood as a bubble of order inside an unlimited ocean of the unformed. That is why the nightly threat to the sun is so serious: if order fails, the water is still there to return. In tomb and papyrus scenes Nun is shown as a man standing waist-deep in water with his arms raised, lifting the solar barque up at dawn.
entities.variantTraditions: The Hermopolitan tradition pairs him with a female counterpart Naunet as one couple of the Ogdoad; the Heliopolitan tradition treats him more simply as the water from which Atum emerged.

entities.name: Atum
entities.role: The self-created; the completed one
entities.worship: The great cult centre was Heliopolis, where the benben stone marked the primeval mound. Atum was invoked especially in royal funerary texts, as the god the dead king joins at the end of the day's course.
entities.bio: The self-created god who rose from Nun on the first mound and made the first pair of gods from himself.
entities.longBio: Atum's name carries both 'the all' and 'the complete', and the tradition uses it in both senses: he is everything that exists in undifferentiated form, and he is what is finished. He brings himself into being on the mound that rises from Nun, and then, having no partner, produces the first pair from his own body - by masturbation in the Pyramid Texts, or by spitting or sneezing them out in versions that later editors evidently found more decorous. Those two are Shu, air, and Tefnut, moisture, and from them the rest of the Ennead descends. Atum is the evening aspect of the sun, the completed daily course, and is regularly fused with Ra as Ra-Atum or Atum-Ra. In one striking passage he tells Osiris that at the end of things he will destroy everything he has made and return with him to the primeval water, the two of them alone in the form of serpents.
entities.variantTraditions: The Heliopolitan account of Atum competes with the Memphite theology, in which Ptah creates by thought and speech and Atum is one of Ptah's products, and with the Hermopolitan Ogdoad. All three were maintained simultaneously.

entities.name: Ra
entities.role: The sun; king of the gods
epithets: Khepri at dawn, Ra at noon, Atum at evening
domains: the daily renewal of the world
entities.abode: The solar barque, crossing the sky by day and the underworld by night
festivals: The daily temple ritual of the sun's rising and setting
entities.worship: Heliopolis was his ancient centre, but solar worship was universal: every temple performed the daily rite that assisted the sun's rebirth, and from the Fifth Dynasty every king took the title Son of Ra.
entities.bio: The sun itself, who sails the sky by day and fights through the underworld each night.
entities.longBio: Ra is the most consistently supreme god of the Egyptian pantheon, and his rule is not a throne but a journey. He crosses the sky in the day barque and at sunset transfers to the night barque, passing through the twelve hours of the underworld, where he is attacked by the serpent Apep and must be defended so that dawn can happen at all. The sun's phases are given separate names and forms - Khepri the scarab at dawn, Ra at midday, Atum at evening - and Egyptian thought treats these as aspects rather than rivals. He is combined freely with other gods: Amun-Ra at Thebes, Ra-Horakhty with Horus, Sobek-Ra. He grows old like a man, which is the premise of two major stories: Isis poisons him to learn his secret name, and mankind rebels against him when he is aged, prompting him to send out his Eye to slaughter them.
entities.variantTraditions: The relationship between Ra and Atum, and between Ra and Amun, varies by period and cult centre; the Amarna period under Akhenaten briefly replaced the whole system with the Aten, the visible disc alone.

entities.name: Khepri
entities.role: The rising sun; the scarab
symbols: the sun disc pushed above the horizon
entities.bio: The sun at dawn, shown as a scarab, whose name means to come into being.
entities.longBio: Egyptians observed the dung beetle rolling its ball across the ground and young beetles apparently emerging from it without a parent, and read the whole thing as a statement about the sun: something round pushed across a surface, and life appearing from within it by itself. Khepri is therefore the sun at the moment of rising, and by extension the principle of coming-into-being. His name is built on the verb kheper, to become, which is one of the most loaded words in the language and appears constantly in creation accounts. He is not usually given a separate cult or mythology, because he is a phase rather than a person - the same god who is Ra at noon and Atum at evening. Scarab amulets were the commonest of all Egyptian amulets, and large heart scarabs were placed with the dead precisely because the beetle carried this promise of self-renewal.
entities.variantTraditions: Khepri is occasionally treated as an independent creator god in his own right, particularly in texts that want a god who came into being by himself without any prior water.

entities.name: Shu
entities.role: Air; the one who holds up the sky
domains: the space between earth and sky
entities.abode: Between Geb and Nut, holding them apart
entities.bio: The first-made god, air itself, who separates the sky from the earth and keeps them apart.
entities.longBio: Atum produces Shu and Tefnut from himself, and Shu is air and the light that fills it. His defining act is a separation: he steps between his children Geb, the earth, and Nut, the sky, who are locked in an embrace, and pushes Nut upward, standing with his arms raised to hold her there. That posture is one of the most reproduced images in Egyptian art, and it makes air the physical condition of there being a world at all - without Shu, sky and earth close again and the space where life happens disappears. He and Tefnut are also identified with the wandering Eye of Ra in some texts, and a story tells of the two of them becoming lost in the waters of Nun and Atum weeping with relief when they are found, the tears becoming humankind by a pun on the words for tears and people.
entities.variantTraditions: In later texts Shu becomes a ruling king of the gods succeeding Ra, and faces his own rebellion; the Greeks sometimes identified him with Atlas for the obvious reason.

entities.name: Tefnut
entities.role: Moisture
domains: the corrosive heat of the sun in another aspect
entities.abode: Heliopolis; and Nubia during her withdrawal
entities.bio: Twin of Shu and the first female principle, moisture, and one form of the Distant Goddess who must be brought home.
entities.longBio: Tefnut is produced with Shu from Atum, and where he is dry air she is moisture - a pairing that in Egypt means the two conditions that make the difference between desert and life. She and Shu are the parents of Geb and Nut, and so the whole Ennead descends through her. Her more dramatic role is as an instance of the Distant Goddess pattern, which recurs across Egyptian religion: the goddess quarrels with her father Ra and withdraws into Nubia in the form of a raging lioness, and while she is absent the land suffers. Thoth is sent to fetch her, and persuades her back by storytelling and flattery rather than force, whereupon she is pacified with music and dance and her return is celebrated as the return of the inundation. The same story is told of Hathor and of Sekhmet, which is a good illustration of how Egyptian deities share functions rather than owning them.
entities.variantTraditions: The Distant Goddess is variously Tefnut, Hathor, Sekhmet, Bastet or Mut depending on the temple telling it; the fullest surviving version is a demotic papyrus about Tefnut.

entities.name: Geb
entities.role: The earth
domains: the tomb that holds the dead
entities.bio: The earth as a male god lying beneath the arched body of the sky, and father of the Osirian generation.
entities.longBio: Egypt inverts the arrangement familiar from Greece and elsewhere: the earth is male and the sky female. Geb lies below, often shown with one knee raised to make the hills, while Nut arches over him supported by Shu. Plants grow from his back, and earthquakes are his laughter - one of his titles is the Great Cackler, connected with the goose he wears on his head and with a tradition that he laid the egg from which the sun hatched. As the father of Osiris, Isis, Set and Nephthys he is the ancestor of the Osirian drama, and as an early king of Egypt in the mythical dynasties he is the one who adjudicates between Horus and Set in some accounts, awarding the throne. Because the dead are placed in the earth, Geb also has a grimmer aspect: he can hold the dead fast, and funerary texts ask him to release them.
entities.variantTraditions: Geb's role in the succession of Horus and Set differs between the Memphite Theology, where he first divides Egypt between them and then reverses himself, and other accounts where the tribunal of gods decides.

entities.name: Nut
entities.role: The sky
domains: the passage of the sun through night
symbols: the arched body studded with stars
the water pot on her head
entities.bio: The sky as a woman arched over the earth, who swallows the sun each evening and gives birth to it each dawn.
entities.longBio: Nut stretches over Geb touching the ground only with fingers and toes, her body the vault of the sky, painted dark blue and covered with stars. The sun enters her mouth at sunset, travels through her body during the night, and is born from her again at dawn, which is why she is painted on the underside of coffin lids and on tomb ceilings: the dead lie beneath her exactly as the sun does, and expect the same outcome. Ra is said to have cursed her not to give birth in any month of the year, and Thoth won five extra days from the moon in a game so that she could bear her five children - Osiris, Horus the Elder, Set, Isis and Nephthys - on days belonging to no month, which is the Egyptian explanation for the five epagomenal days added to the 360-day calendar.
entities.variantTraditions: The five-days story is preserved most fully by Plutarch and may be a Greek-period systematisation of older material; the number and names of her children vary.

entities.name: Osiris
entities.role: Lord of the dead; the murdered and risen king
entities.abode: The Duat, as its king; Abydos, where his head was buried
festivals: The Mysteries of Osiris at Abydos, an annual passion play
the Khoiak festival of the corn mummy
entities.worship: Abydos was the great pilgrimage centre, believed to hold his head, and Egyptians of all classes set up memorial stelae there to share in the festival. Corn mummies - Osiris shapes filled with soil and grain - were made and watered so that the sprouting seed enacted his return.
entities.bio: The king murdered by his brother, reassembled by his wife, and made ruler of the dead rather than the living.
entities.longBio: Osiris rules Egypt as a good king, teaching agriculture and law, until his brother Set kills him - by trapping him in a coffin at a banquet, in Plutarch's version, or by drowning or dismemberment in Egyptian sources. Isis recovers the body; Set finds it again and cuts it into pieces scattered across Egypt, and Isis, with Nephthys, gathers them. What she cannot find is the phallus, eaten by a fish, so she fashions a replacement, and by magic conceives Horus from the reassembled body. Osiris does not return to the living world. He becomes king of the Duat, and it is his son who reclaims the earthly throne. This is the central pattern of Egyptian religion: the dead king becomes Osiris and the living king is Horus, so every succession repeats the myth, and every ordinary dead person hoped to be identified with Osiris and so to live on.
entities.variantTraditions: Plutarch preserves the fullest connected narrative but writes centuries later and in Greek terms; Egyptian sources give the episodes scattered across funerary texts and rarely tell it straight through. The number of pieces Set cut him into is given as fourteen, sixteen or forty-two in different sources.

entities.name: Isis
entities.role: The great enchantress; wife of Osiris, mother of Horus
epithets: Mistress of the Words of Power
symbols: the throne hieroglyph on her head
entities.abode: Everywhere she is invoked; Philae, her last temple
festivals: The Navigium Isidis in the Roman period
the Osiris mysteries, where she is chief mourner
entities.worship: Her Egyptian cult grew steadily and outlasted the rest: the temple at Philae was the last functioning Egyptian temple, closed only in the sixth century CE. In the Roman empire she had temples from London to the Euphrates.
entities.bio: The most capable figure in Egyptian myth: she reassembles her murdered husband, conceives his heir, and protects him until he can claim the throne.
entities.longBio: Isis' name is written with the throne sign, and the identification is exact - she is the seat of kingship, and the king is legitimate because he sits on her. When Osiris is killed she searches for him, finds him, and when the body is dismembered she gathers the pieces and restores them enough to conceive Horus. She then hides in the marshes of Chemmis raising the child in secret from Set, and when the infant is stung by a scorpion she stops the solar barque itself and refuses to let it move until Ra sends Thoth to help her cure him. Her most famous act is a piece of pure leverage: she makes a serpent from Ra's own spittle and the earth, lets it bite him, and refuses to cure the aged god unless he tells her his secret name, which she then holds. In the Greco-Roman period her cult spread across the entire Mediterranean.
entities.variantTraditions: Plutarch's account differs in many details from Egyptian sources, and the wanderings of Isis to Byblos appear only in him. Her assimilation to Greek Demeter and Aphrodite, and later comparisons with the Virgin Mary, belong to the reception rather than to Egyptian religion.

entities.name: Set
entities.role: God of the desert, storm and disorder
domains: the defence of the solar barque
symbols: the Set animal, an unidentified beast
entities.abode: The red desert; and the prow of the night barque
entities.worship: Ombos and Avaris were his centres, and he was genuinely popular in the eastern Delta and among the Ramesside kings, several of whom took his name. Later his images were erased in many temples.
entities.bio: Osiris' brother and murderer, god of the desert and storm, and also the strongest defender of the sun.
entities.longBio: Set is the most morally complicated god in the pantheon, and reading him as a simple devil is a Greek and later distortion. He murders Osiris and contests the throne with Horus in a struggle lasting eighty years - a contest that includes lawsuits before the tribunal of gods, transformations into hippopotami, and an episode of sexual humiliation that Horus turns back on him with Isis' help. He is finally defeated and the throne goes to Horus. But Set is also indispensable: he stands in the prow of Ra's night barque and spears Apep, and he is the only god strong enough to do it. Egyptians of the Nineteenth Dynasty named kings after him. What he embodies is not evil but the necessary violence and disorder at the edge of things - the desert that is not the Nile valley, the storm, the foreigner - and only in the Late Period, under foreign rule, does he harden into a straightforward enemy.
entities.variantTraditions: The Set animal has never been identified with any real species. His demonisation grows late, and in the Third Intermediate Period his images were sometimes defaced; the Greeks identified him with Typhon.

entities.name: Nephthys
entities.role: Lady of the house; mourner of the dead
symbols: the house-and-basket hieroglyph on her head
entities.abode: Beside her sister at every bier
entities.bio: Sister of Isis and wife of Set, who nonetheless helps Isis recover Osiris and mourns beside her.
entities.longBio: Nephthys is the fourth of Nut's children and the least independently characterised, which is partly the point: her role is to accompany. She is married to Set, but takes Isis' side after the murder, helping search for the body and standing at the other end of the bier as the second of the two kites who mourn Osiris. The pairing of the two sisters at the head and foot of the coffin becomes a fixed element of funerary art, and the wailing of the kite was imitated in the ritual lament. In one strand of tradition she conceives Anubis by Osiris, having disguised herself as Isis, and abandons the child, whom Isis raises - a story that gives Anubis a place in the family and Nephthys a rare moment of initiative. She is generally the darker and more nocturnal of the pair, associated with the edge of things rather than their centre.
entities.variantTraditions: The parentage of Anubis is inconsistent; older sources make him a son of Ra, and the Nephthys version is attested mainly through Plutarch and later Egyptian material.

entities.name: Horus
entities.role: The falcon; the living king
entities.abode: Edfu; and the throne of Egypt in every reign
festivals: The Festival of the Beautiful Meeting at Edfu
the coronation rites of each new king
entities.worship: Edfu preserves the most complete surviving Egyptian temple, and its walls carry the fullest account of Horus' victory over Set, performed there as an annual ritual drama.
entities.bio: Son of Isis and Osiris, who contests the throne with Set for eighty years and wins it.
entities.longBio: Horus is really several figures the tradition ran together: Horus the Elder, a sky god whose eyes are the sun and moon and who is a brother of Osiris; and Horus the Child, Harpocrates, son of Isis and Osiris, raised in hiding in the marshes. It is the second who fights Set. The Contendings of Horus and Set is a long, strange and sometimes comic text in which the two are repeatedly judged by the tribunal of gods, transform into hippopotami, and try to disqualify each other, until Osiris himself intervenes from the underworld and the throne is awarded to Horus. In the fighting Set tears out Horus' eye, which is healed by Thoth or Hathor; the restored Eye of Horus, the wedjat, becomes the standard Egyptian symbol of wholeness and healing and the commonest of all amulets. Every living pharaoh was Horus, and every dead one Osiris.
entities.variantTraditions: The multiplication of Horus forms - Horus the Elder, Harsiese, Harpocrates, Horus of Behdet, Ra-Horakhty - reflects the merging of several originally separate falcon gods, and the sources do not always distinguish them.

entities.name: Amun
entities.role: The hidden one; king of the gods at Thebes
epithets: Lord of the Thrones of the Two Lands
domains: the unseen power behind all things
festivals: Opet festival, carrying his image from Karnak to Luxor
the Beautiful Festival of the Valley
entities.worship: Karnak and Luxor were his great houses, and the Opet procession annually renewed the king's divine legitimacy. His oracle at Siwa in the western desert was consulted from across the Mediterranean.
entities.bio: One of the Ogdoad who rose to become the supreme state god of the New Kingdom.
entities.longBio: Amun begins as one of the eight Hermopolitan powers, paired with Amaunet, and his name means the hidden or concealed one - a god defined by not being visible, which made him unusually adaptable. When Theban princes drove out the Hyksos and founded the New Kingdom, their local god rose with them, fused with the sun as Amun-Ra, and became the imperial deity of Egypt at its most powerful. Karnak grew into the largest religious structure ever built. His priesthood became so wealthy and politically strong that it eventually rivalled the throne, and Akhenaten's suppression of Amun in favour of the Aten is usually read partly as a move against that power. After Akhenaten's death the reaction was total: his monuments were dismantled and Amun restored. A hymn describes him as one whose true form is unknown even to the other gods, which is his theological character exactly.
entities.variantTraditions: The Amun of Thebes and the Amun of the Ogdoad were reconciled by the priesthood rather than being originally the same; Greeks identified him with Zeus, and the oracle at Siwa that Alexander consulted was his.

entities.name: Amaunet
entities.role: The hidden one, female
entities.bio: Female counterpart of Amun among the eight, and an early Theban goddess in her own right.
entities.longBio: The Ogdoad is built of four male-female pairs, each expressing one quality of the state before creation, and Amaunet is the female half of hiddenness. Unlike most of the eight she had a real independent cult at Thebes, attested from the Old Kingdom, and she appears in coronation scenes at Karnak. As Amun rose to imperial status, however, his consort role was largely taken over by Mut, and Amaunet receded into a mostly ceremonial presence. The eight are shown as frogs (male) and snakes (female), creatures of the wet silt, which is a precise piece of observation: they represent the qualities of the primordial mud from which the first mound emerged.
entities.variantTraditions: Amaunet is sometimes conflated with Neith, and at Thebes her position as Amun's consort was displaced by Mut without either goddess being removed.

entities.name: Heh and Hauhet
entities.role: Endlessness
symbols: a kneeling man holding two palm ribs
entities.bio: The Ogdoad pair expressing infinity, and the standard Egyptian image for a wish of endless years.
entities.longBio: Heh and his consort Hauhet embody limitlessness - not eternity in the sense of timelessness, but extent without boundary. Heh's image, a kneeling figure holding a notched palm rib in each hand with a shen ring at his feet, became the standard hieroglyphic way of writing a very large number and of wishing a king millions of years of life, so he appears constantly in royal iconography quite apart from any myth. Tutankhamun's tomb goods carry him repeatedly. He also appears in the group of eight who lift the solar barque. As with the rest of the Ogdoad he has no narrative: these are conditions, not characters, and their function is to describe what the world was like before anything happened in it.
entities.variantTraditions: Heh is sometimes confused with Huh, and his sign is also used for the number one million; his role differs entirely between the Hermopolitan theology and royal iconography.

entities.name: Kek and Kauket
entities.role: Darkness
entities.bio: The Ogdoad pair expressing the darkness that preceded the first light.
entities.longBio: Kek and Kauket are the darkness of the pre-creation state, and their titles are unexpectedly hopeful: Kek is called bringer of the light and Kauket bringer of the night, because the darkness before dawn is understood as the condition that makes dawn possible rather than as an enemy of it. This is a characteristically Egyptian move - the primordial state is not evil, only unformed, and the real adversary is Apep, who attacks the ordered world after it exists. Like all the Ogdoad they are depicted as a frog-headed man and a snake-headed woman, and they have no stories, only a place in the account of what was there before Atum rose.
entities.variantTraditions: The Hermopolitan Ogdoad competes with the Heliopolitan Ennead and the Memphite theology; Egyptian religion never chose between them.

entities.name: Thoth
entities.role: God of writing, reckoning and the moon
festivals: The festival of Thoth opening the first month of the year
entities.worship: Hermopolis was his city, where mummified ibises were dedicated in enormous numbers. Scribes poured out a drop of water to him before starting work, and his House of Life attached to temples was where texts were copied and taught.
entities.bio: Ibis-headed god of writing and measure, who records the verdict at the weighing of the heart.
entities.longBio: Thoth invents writing, which the Egyptians regarded as the most consequential gift any god made, and he is the scribe and arbitrator of the divine court. He records the result at the weighing of the heart, standing beside the scales with his palette. His interventions repeatedly rescue the situation when force cannot: he wins five extra days from the moon so Nut can bear her children; he is sent to fetch the Distant Goddess home from Nubia, and persuades her with stories rather than power; he heals the eye of Horus, which is why the restored wedjat is a symbol of wholeness; and he cures the infant Horus of scorpion venom when Isis has stopped the solar barque in her distress. As lord of measure he governs the calendar, the reckoning of time and the boundaries of fields, and priests of the House of Life worked under him.
entities.variantTraditions: The Greeks identified Thoth with Hermes, and the fusion produced Hermes Trismegistus, the supposed author of the Hermetic writings - a Greco-Egyptian construct of the Roman period, not an Egyptian god.

entities.name: Ptah
entities.role: Creator by thought and speech; patron of craftsmen
epithets: He Who Is South of His Wall
entities.worship: Memphis was his city and one of the greatest temple complexes in Egypt. Craftsmen's guilds honoured him, and the Apis bull kept in his precinct was consulted as an oracle.
entities.bio: The Memphite creator who makes the world by conceiving it in his heart and speaking it with his tongue.
entities.longBio: The Shabaka Stone preserves the Memphite Theology, and it is one of the most intellectually striking texts to survive from the ancient world: Ptah creates not by physical act but by thinking a thing in his heart and naming it with his tongue, and the other gods including Atum are among the things so made. This puts a theory of mind and language at the origin of the cosmos more than two millennia before comparable Greek formulations. Ptah is also the patron of craftsmen, sculptors and metalworkers - the same principle applied at human scale, giving shape to material - and the high priest of Memphis carried the title Greatest of Directors of Craftsmen. Fused with Sokar and Osiris as Ptah-Sokar-Osiris, he becomes a funerary composite. The Apis bull was regarded as his living manifestation.
entities.variantTraditions: The Shabaka Stone claims to copy a worm-eaten older document; whether the theology is genuinely Old Kingdom or a later Memphite claim to priority over Heliopolis is debated. The Greek name Aigyptos, and so Egypt, may derive from hut-ka-ptah, the house of the ka of Ptah.

entities.name: Hathor
entities.role: Goddess of love, music, joy and the sky
symbols: cow horns with a sun disc
festivals: the Beautiful Reunion, when her image sailed to Edfu to meet Horus
entities.worship: Dendera preserves a nearly complete temple. Women in particular dedicated to her, and her festivals involved music, beer and deliberate intoxication as a religious act.
entities.bio: Goddess of joy and music, nurse of the king, and in her other aspect the raging Eye of Ra.
entities.longBio: Hathor's name means house of Horus, and she is the sky as the enclosure that contains the sun, often shown as a cow with the disc between her horns. Her domains are the ones Egyptians most enjoyed: love, music, dancing, drunkenness and celebration, and her festivals were correspondingly loud. She nurses the king, meets the dead at the edge of the desert as Mistress of the West, and offers shade and water from the sycamore. But she carries the other side of the same energy. When Ra grows old and mankind plots against him, he sends his Eye as Hathor to punish them, and she becomes Sekhmet and slaughters so enthusiastically that Ra repents and has beer dyed red with ochre poured over the fields; she drinks it believing it blood, becomes drunk, and stops. That story is the charter of her drunkenness festival.
entities.variantTraditions: Hathor, Sekhmet, Bastet, Tefnut and Mut are all identified at times as the Eye of Ra and shade into one another; Dendera's temple carries the fullest surviving Hathor material.

entities.name: Sekhmet
entities.role: The powerful one; lioness of plague and healing
domains: the destroying heat of the sun
festivals: The Festival of Drunkenness, commemorating her pacification
entities.worship: Her priests, the wabau of Sekhmet, functioned as a medical order. Litanies were recited before her many statues to keep the plague-bringing aspect appeased.
entities.bio: Lioness goddess of the sun's destroying heat, who nearly wiped out humankind and was stopped with beer.
entities.longBio: Sekhmet is what the Eye of Ra becomes when it is sent to kill. In the Book of the Heavenly Cow, mankind plots against the aged Ra and he despatches his Eye; as Sekhmet she massacres them across the desert and cannot be recalled, having acquired a taste for it. Ra has seven thousand jars of beer dyed red with ochre poured out over the fields at Dendera; she drinks, believing it blood, falls asleep, and humanity survives. Her arrows are plague - the annual epidemics were called the messengers of Sekhmet - but by exactly the same logic she can withhold them, so her priests were physicians and her cult was a medical one. Amenhotep III installed hundreds of granite statues of her at Thebes, apparently one for each day of the year, so that the litany could be recited continuously.
entities.variantTraditions: Sekhmet, Hathor and Bastet are aspects of one pattern rather than separate goddesses in many texts; the pacification story is told of each.

entities.name: Anubis
entities.role: Jackal god of embalming and the necropolis
epithets: He Who Is Upon His Mountain
entities.abode: The necropolis, on the edge of the desert
entities.worship: Cynopolis was his centre, and vast dog and jackal catacombs were filled with mummified animals dedicated to him. Every embalming workshop operated under his patronage.
entities.bio: The jackal who invented embalming, guards the cemetery, and operates the scales at the judgment.
entities.longBio: Anubis is the oldest of the funerary gods, dominant before Osiris took over the underworld, after which he keeps the practical offices: he embalms, he guards, and he weighs. He is jackal-headed because jackals scavenged at desert cemeteries, and the Egyptian response was to make the animal that threatened the dead into their protector - a characteristic inversion. He conducts the first embalming, on Osiris, which makes him the patron of the practice, and embalmers wore his mask during the ritual. At the judgment he leads the deceased in by the hand, adjusts the scales, and reports the reading to Thoth. His black colour is not the jackal's but the black of fertile silt and of the embalmed body, signalling regeneration rather than death.
entities.variantTraditions: His parentage varies: a son of Ra in older texts, of Nephthys by Osiris in later ones, or of Set in a few. The Greeks merged him with Hermes as Hermanubis.

entities.name: Maat
entities.role: Truth, order and the balance of the world
domains: the balance against which a life is weighed
entities.abode: The hall of judgment; and every properly governed thing
entities.worship: Rarely given large temples of her own; instead she is present in the judgment hall, in the courts, and in the daily offering the king makes to the gods.
entities.bio: The principle of order and truth, personified as a goddess and weighed against the heart of the dead.
entities.longBio: Maat is the most important idea in Egyptian religion and only secondarily a goddess. She is the rightness of things: the sun rising on time, the Nile flooding, the king judging fairly, a person dealing honestly. Her opposite is isfet, chaos and falsehood. The whole purpose of kingship is to uphold maat, which is why kings are shown offering a small figure of her to the gods - the offering of order itself, the only gift that matters. At death the heart is weighed against her single ostrich feather, and the forty-two negative confessions in the Book of the Dead are a declaration of having lived by her. She is called the daughter of Ra and is said to be what he lives on. Judges wore her image, and the vizier held the title priest of Maat.
entities.variantTraditions: Maat is sometimes doubled as the Two Maats presiding over the judgment hall; the concept is far more prominent in the texts than the personified goddess.

entities.name: Bastet
entities.role: Cat goddess of home, fertility and protection
domains: protection from disease and evil spirits
festivals: The festival at Bubastis, described by Herodotus as the greatest in Egypt
entities.worship: Bubastis was her city. Bronze cat statuettes were among the commonest votive offerings in Egypt, and mummified cats were dedicated by the hundreds of thousands.
entities.bio: The cat goddess: the Eye of Ra in her pacified, protective form rather than her raging one.
entities.longBio: Bastet begins as a lioness like Sekhmet and softens, from the second millennium onward, into the domestic cat - the same solar power in a form that guards the house rather than destroying armies. Egyptians valued cats for killing snakes, scorpions and vermin, and the goddess carries that protective function into the supernatural: she wards the home, guards women in childbirth, and defends against disease and malign spirits. Her festival at Bubastis was, according to Herodotus, the largest and most uninhibited in Egypt, drawing hundreds of thousands who travelled by barge singing, clapping and drinking far more wine than at any other time of year. Cat cemeteries at Bubastis and Saqqara held enormous numbers of mummified cats offered to her, bred for the purpose.
entities.variantTraditions: The pairing of Bastet as the gentle Eye and Sekhmet as the fierce one is a later systematisation; earlier Bastet is straightforwardly leonine.

entities.name: Sobek
entities.role: Crocodile god of the Nile, fertility and military power
entities.worship: The Faiyum and Kom Ombo were his centres. Sacred crocodiles were kept, adorned and fed in temple lakes, and crocodile mummies were dedicated in large numbers.
entities.bio: Crocodile god of the river's fertility and its menace, who is appeased rather than defeated.
entities.longBio: Sobek is the Nile crocodile made a god, and the logic is the same as with Anubis and the jackal: the thing that kills you at the water's edge is turned into the power that protects you there. He is credited with the fertility that the flood brings, and his sweat was said to have formed the river. Pharaohs of the Twelfth Dynasty, several named Amenemhat, developed the Faiyum where he was strongest, and in the Thirteenth Dynasty kings took the name Sobekhotep and Sobekneferu. Fused with the sun as Sobek-Ra, he acquires a solar dimension. Live crocodiles were kept in temple pools at Crocodilopolis and at Kom Ombo, decorated with gold and glass ornaments, fed by visitors, and mummified at death; Kom Ombo's temple is unusual in being split in two, one half for Sobek and one for Horus the Elder.
entities.variantTraditions: Sobek's relationship with Set is inconsistent - sometimes an ally of the disorder Set represents, sometimes a defender of Ra against exactly that.

entities.name: Apep
entities.role: The serpent of chaos who attacks the sun
domains: the nightly threat to the sun
entities.abode: The Duat, in the waters the solar barque must cross
entities.bio: The vast serpent who attacks Ra's barque every night and must be repelled every night.
entities.longBio: Apep is the closest thing Egyptian religion has to a devil, and the difference from a devil is instructive: he wants nothing, rules nothing, and offers nothing. He is unbeing, and his sole activity is to swallow the sun. Each night as the solar barque passes through the Duat he attacks, and the crew - with Set standing in the prow with a spear, which is the clearest statement of why Set cannot simply be an enemy - fights him off. He is never destroyed, only driven back, and the fight recurs the following night without end. Storms, unseasonal darkness and eclipses were explained as moments when he nearly succeeded. Temples performed rites called Overthrowing Apep, in which wax figures of the serpent were named, spat on, cut with knives, and burned, and the surviving Books of Overthrowing Apep are among the most vivid ritual texts from Egypt.
entities.variantTraditions: Apep is essentially absent from the Old Kingdom Pyramid Texts and grows in importance later, which suggests a developing rather than an original figure.

entities.name: Ammit
entities.role: Devourer of the unworthy dead
entities.abode: Beside the scales in the hall of judgment
entities.bio: Part crocodile, lion and hippopotamus; she eats the heart that fails the weighing.
entities.longBio: Ammit crouches beside the scales in every illustrated judgment scene, composed of the three animals Egyptians considered most lethal - the crocodile's head, the lion's chest and forelegs, the hippopotamus' hindquarters. She does not torment anyone and is not a ruler of any place. If the heart outweighs the feather of Maat she eats it, and the consequence is not punishment but cessation: the person simply stops existing, which to Egyptian thought was the worst possible outcome, far worse than suffering. There is no hell in the Egyptian system in the sense of ongoing torment for the ordinary dead; there is continued existence, which requires passing the test and being maintained by offerings, and there is Ammit. She is never worshipped and has no cult, existing purely as the stake in the wager.
entities.variantTraditions: Some texts place the devouring at a lake of fire instead, and the details of the judgment vary across copies of the Book of the Dead.

entities.name: Taweret
entities.role: Hippopotamus goddess of childbirth
domains: warding off harm from the household
symbols: hippopotamus body with lion's paws and a crocodile's back
entities.abode: The birth house, and every bedroom
entities.worship: Domestic rather than temple religion: amulets, apotropaic wands and bed decorations, found throughout settlements at every social level.
entities.bio: Pregnant hippopotamus goddess who guards women in labour and newborn children.
entities.longBio: Taweret is built from three dangerous animals - hippopotamus, lion and crocodile - and turned entirely to protection, standing upright with a swollen belly and heavy breasts, often leaning on the sa sign of protection or holding a torch whose flame drives off evil. She has almost no mythology and was among the most present of all Egyptian deities in ordinary life: her image appears on beds, headrests, cosmetic jars, wands and amulets in enormous numbers, in workmen's houses as much as palaces, because childbirth was the most dangerous ordinary event a person faced. She was believed to attend the birth, frighten off the spirits that threatened mother and child, and continue guarding the infant afterwards. The female hippopotamus, famously aggressive in defence of her young, is the whole logic of the figure.
entities.variantTraditions: The male hippopotamus by contrast was associated with Set and hunted ritually; the same animal carries opposite meanings depending on its sex.

entities.name: Bes
entities.role: Dwarf god of the household, childbirth and joy
domains: driving off snakes and evil spirits
entities.worship: Purely domestic and popular: amulets, furniture, and birth-house decoration. Later there were Bes chambers where people slept seeking healing dreams.
entities.bio: A grotesque, cheerful dwarf who guards the home and frightens away what threatens it.
entities.longBio: Bes breaks every Egyptian artistic convention and does it deliberately. Where gods are shown in dignified profile, he faces forward, squat and bandy-legged, with a lion's mane, a protruding tongue and often a comic expression. That ugliness is the point: he frightens away hostile spirits, snakes and scorpions by being more alarming than they are. He is a household god rather than a temple one, present on beds, mirrors, headrests and cosmetic articles, and he dances and plays the tambourine at births to scare off whatever might harm the child. He and Taweret work the same territory and appear together constantly. His popularity was enormous and long-lived, spreading well beyond Egypt into Nubia, the Levant and the Roman world, where he turns up on amulets far from any Egyptian temple.
entities.variantTraditions: Bes may be a group of similar dwarf deities rather than one, and his origin - Egyptian, Nubian or Near Eastern - is unresolved.

entities.name: The Bennu
entities.role: The heron of rebirth; the phoenix
epithets: He Who Came Into Being By Himself
entities.bio: The heron that alighted on the first mound at creation, and the origin of the phoenix.
entities.longBio: The Bennu is said to have flown over the waters of Nun and alighted on the benben, the primeval mound at Heliopolis, and its cry broke the original silence and determined what would and would not be. It is a grey heron with two long plumes, and it is called the ba - the soul - of Ra, so that its appearance is the sun's own renewal. Its association with cycles of time made it the marker of long periods and of jubilee festivals. Greek writers, above all Herodotus, reported the Egyptian bird as the phoenix, adding the detail of a bird that returns to Heliopolis every five hundred years bearing its dead parent encased in myrrh, and later authors supplied the self-immolation and rebirth from ashes that the Egyptian bird does not have.
entities.variantTraditions: The self-burning phoenix is a Greek and later elaboration; the Egyptian Bennu renews without fire. Some texts make it the ba of Osiris rather than of Ra.

entities.name: Apis
entities.role: The living bull of Ptah
domains: the living presence of a god
symbols: a black bull with a white triangle on the forehead
the sun disc between the horns
entities.abode: The Apis stall at Memphis; the Serapeum at Saqqara after death
entities.worship: The Apis stall at Memphis and the Serapeum at Saqqara. Its installation, oracles and funeral were state occasions.
entities.bio: A living bull identified by specific markings and kept as the visible manifestation of Ptah.
entities.longBio: The Apis is unusual in being an actual animal rather than an image: when the bull died, priests searched Egypt for a calf bearing the required markings - black with a white triangular blaze on the forehead, a crescent on the flank, and other signs - and the calf found was installed at Memphis with its mother, housed in luxury, and treated as the god's living herald. Its movements were read as oracles, and people came to put questions to it. On its death it was mummified with the full apparatus of a royal burial and interred in the Serapeum at Saqqara, a vast underground gallery of granite sarcophagi that Mariette rediscovered in 1851. The Ptolemies fused Apis and Osiris into Serapis, a deliberately Greco-Egyptian god designed to be worshipped by both communities.
entities.variantTraditions: The exact list of required markings differs between ancient authors. Cambyses was accused by Herodotus of stabbing the Apis, a story Egyptian evidence does not support.

entities.name: Imhotep
entities.role: Architect, physician, and a mortal who became a god
entities.abode: Memphis; and the healing sanctuary at Saqqara
entities.worship: Healing sanctuaries at Saqqara, Memphis and Philae practised incubation. Scribes honoured him as a patron of their craft.
entities.bio: The real architect of the Step Pyramid, deified fifteen centuries after his death as a god of medicine.
entities.longBio: Imhotep is one of very few non-royal Egyptians to become a god, and unlike most mythological figures he demonstrably existed: he was chancellor to King Djoser of the Third Dynasty and the architect of the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the first monumental stone building in the world, and his name and titles appear on a statue base of Djoser. Remembered afterwards as the model of the wise man, he was credited with medical knowledge, and by the Late Period he had been fully deified as a son of Ptah and a god of healing, with sanctuaries where the sick slept seeking cures in dreams - the same incubation practice as at Greek Asclepius shrines, and the Greeks duly identified the two. Scribes poured a libation to him before writing. His tomb has never been found.
entities.variantTraditions: The Edwin Smith surgical papyrus is sometimes attributed to him, but the attribution is speculative and the surviving copy is far later.

entities.name: Mut
entities.role: Mother goddess; consort of Amun at Thebes
entities.worship: The Mut precinct at Karnak, with its horseshoe lake, held hundreds of Sekhmet statues and hosted a festival of drunkenness of its own.
entities.bio: Consort of Amun and mother of Khonsu, forming the Theban triad.
entities.longBio: Mut's name is simply the word for mother, written with the vulture sign, and she rose alongside Amun as Thebes rose. With Amun and their son Khonsu she forms the Theban triad, the family group that anchored the city's theology, and her precinct at Karnak surrounds a crescent-shaped sacred lake called the Isheru. Like Hathor and Sekhmet she has a leonine aspect and appears as one of the forms of the raging Eye of Ra that must be pacified. The vulture headdress she wears became the standard headgear of Egyptian queens, which is the point: Mut is queenship as an institution, and the living queen participates in her. Hatshepsut and later rulers built substantially in her precinct.
entities.variantTraditions: Mut displaced Amaunet as Amun's consort without Amaunet being removed from the Ogdoad; both arrangements coexisted.

entities.name: Khonsu
entities.role: The traveller; moon god of Thebes
entities.bio: Moon god and third member of the Theban triad, credited with healing and driving out spirits.
entities.longBio: Khonsu's name comes from a verb meaning to cross or traverse, describing the moon's journey across the night sky. Son of Amun and Mut, he completes the Theban triad and has a well-preserved temple within the Karnak complex. His reputation was as a healer and an expeller of hostile spirits, and the Bentresh Stela records a story in which his image is sent to a foreign court to cure a princess possessed by a spirit - a text probably composed centuries after the reign it claims to describe, but which shows exactly what people expected of him. In earlier material he has a much fiercer character, appearing in the Pyramid Texts as a bloodthirsty deity who helps the king devour other gods, a side that faded entirely later.
entities.variantTraditions: The Bentresh Stela is a pious fiction of the Late Period presented as a New Kingdom document; the ferocity of the Pyramid Text Khonsu is hard to reconcile with the later healer.

entities.name: The Aten
entities.role: The visible disc of the sun
domains: light as the source of all life
symbols: the disc with rays ending in hands
the ankh offered to the royal family
entities.worship: Open-air temples at Akhetaten with no roof and no cult statue, so that the sun itself fell on the offerings. Abandoned within a generation.
entities.bio: The sun-disc itself, briefly raised by Akhenaten to be the only god of Egypt.
entities.longBio: The Aten begins as an ordinary word for the sun's disc and as a minor aspect of the solar cult, then becomes the centre of the most radical episode in Egyptian religious history. Amenhotep IV renamed himself Akhenaten, moved the capital to a new city at Akhetaten, and promoted the Aten as the sole deity, closing temples and having the name of Amun chiselled out across Egypt. The Aten is never shown as a person or animal, only as a disc whose rays end in small hands holding the ankh, and those hands reach only the royal family - the king was the sole intermediary, which made the theology and the politics the same move. The Great Hymn to the Aten is a genuinely remarkable poem about a god who makes the chick speak in the egg and gives every land its own Nile in the sky. After Akhenaten's death everything was reversed and his city abandoned.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether Atenism was true monotheism or the elevation of one god above others is debated, as is the frequently drawn comparison between the Great Hymn and Psalm 104.

entities.name: Min
entities.role: God of fertility, the eastern desert and virility
festivals: The Festival of the Coming Forth of Min, at the start of the harvest
entities.bio: Ancient fertility god shown ithyphallic, patron of the eastern desert routes and of the harvest.
entities.longBio: Min is among the oldest attested Egyptian gods, appearing on Predynastic objects, and he is depicted with unvarying directness: mummiform, one arm raised holding a flail, erect. His domain is generative force, and the tall romaine lettuce sacred to him was eaten as an aphrodisiac because of the milky sap it exudes. His cities, Coptos and Akhmim, sat at the head of the desert roads to the Red Sea, so he also became the protector of mining and quarrying expeditions into the eastern desert. His great festival came at the start of the harvest: the king cut the first sheaf of emmer in his presence, tying the god's fertility directly to the year's grain and to the king's own potency. He is frequently fused with Amun as Amun-Min.
entities.variantTraditions: Greek writers identified him with Pan, and Akhmim was called Panopolis; Min is also merged with Horus in some contexts as Min-Horus.

entities.name: Neith
entities.role: Goddess of weaving, war and the primeval waters
entities.worship: Sais was her city, and the Twenty-Sixth Dynasty made it the capital, raising her cult to national prominence.
entities.bio: One of the oldest goddesses: weaver, warrior, and in some accounts the creator of the world.
entities.longBio: Neith is attested from the First Dynasty and combines domains that later gods divide: she weaves, which in Egyptian thought is close to creating, and she is a warrior with bow and arrows. At Sais her theology made her the primeval creator who emerged from Nun and brought the world into being, weaving it as she wove linen, and who created Ra as her son - a claim as absolute as anything at Heliopolis or Memphis. She arbitrates in the Contendings of Horus and Set, sending a letter to the tribunal proposing that the throne go to Horus and Set be compensated with two foreign goddesses. As one of the four protective goddesses she guards the canopic jars with Isis, Nephthys and Serqet, and the mummy wrappings themselves fall under her as goddess of weaving.
entities.variantTraditions: The Greeks identified Neith with Athena, and Plato's Timaeus has the Atlantis story reported by priests at Sais, her city.

entities.name: Seshat
entities.role: Goddess of writing, measurement and records
epithets: Mistress of the House of Books
symbols: the seven-pointed emblem above her head
the palm rib notched for years
entities.abode: The House of Life, and the foundation of every temple
entities.bio: Female counterpart of Thoth, who measures out temple foundations and records the years of a reign.
entities.longBio: Seshat performs the stretching of the cord, the ritual in which the king and the goddess mark out the ground plan of a new temple with pegs and a measuring line aligned to the stars - the moment a building becomes possible - and she appears in that scene from the earliest dynasties onward. She also writes the king's name on the leaves of the ished tree and notches a palm rib to record the years granted to his reign, and she keeps the inventory of foreign booty. Her emblem is a seven-pointed star or rosette beneath a bow shape whose meaning has never been established. She is variously called the daughter, sister or consort of Thoth, and where he is the inventor of writing she is the keeper of what is written.
entities.variantTraditions: The reading of her headdress emblem is unsolved; suggestions range from a papyrus plant to a star to a stylised bow, and none is secure.

entities.name: Khnum
entities.role: The potter who shapes bodies on his wheel
domains: the shaping of bodies and the ka
symbols: the ram's head with wavy horns
entities.worship: Elephantine and Esna were his centres, with a triad of Khnum, Satis and Anuket governing the cataract region.
entities.bio: Ram-headed god who moulds each child and its ka on a potter's wheel before birth.
entities.longBio: Khnum guards the cataract at Aswan where the Nile was believed to enter Egypt, and the annual inundation was thought to issue from caverns under his control - a position of extraordinary practical importance, since the flood decided whether the country ate. His other role is intimate rather than national: he forms each human being on a potter's wheel out of Nile clay, shaping the body and the ka together and placing them in the mother's womb, which appears in temple birth scenes where he moulds the infant king and the royal ka side by side. The Famine Stela on Sehel Island records a seven-year famine ended when Djoser restored Khnum's temple, a text carved in the Ptolemaic period but claiming Old Kingdom authority.
entities.variantTraditions: The Famine Stela is a Ptolemaic composition asserting an ancient land grant to the priesthood, not a contemporary Third Dynasty record.

entities.name: Wadjet
entities.role: Cobra goddess of Lower Egypt
domains: the uraeus that spits fire at enemies
entities.bio: The cobra who rears on the king's brow, patron of Lower Egypt and half of the Two Ladies.
entities.longBio: Wadjet is the uraeus, the rearing cobra worn at the front of the royal headdress, and her function is direct: she spits fire at whoever approaches the king with harm in mind. As patron of Lower Egypt she pairs with Nekhbet the vulture of Upper Egypt to form the Two Ladies, one of the five great titles of every pharaoh and the clearest statement of the unified kingdom in the royal titulary. She is counted among the forms of the Eye of Ra, which is what gives her the fire. In the Osiris story she is one of those who shelter Isis and the infant Horus in the marshes of Chemmis. Her name means the green one, from the papyrus that grew across her Delta homeland.
entities.variantTraditions: The wedjat eye of Horus and the goddess Wadjet are etymologically related and often conflated in amulet contexts, though they are distinct.

entities.name: Nekhbet
entities.role: Vulture goddess of Upper Egypt
symbols: the shen ring in her talons
entities.bio: The vulture of Upper Egypt, who with Wadjet forms the Two Ladies of the royal titulary.
entities.longBio: Nekhbet spreads her wings above the king in protection, often shown hovering over the throne clutching the shen ring of eternity. As patron of Upper Egypt she is the southern half of the Two Ladies, and the vulture and cobra heads appear side by side on the royal brow when both kingdoms are meant. Her association with vultures gave her a maternal character rather than a grim one, since Egyptians observed the bird's attentive care of its young, and she is called mother of mothers and shown as a nurse to the king. The vulture headdress worn by queens is hers. Her city Nekheb sits opposite Nekhen, Hierakonpolis, one of the oldest centres of kingship in Egypt, which explains her closeness to the throne.
entities.variantTraditions: The Greeks identified her with Eileithyia, the goddess of childbirth, and called her city Eileithyiaspolis.

entities.name: Serqet
entities.role: Scorpion goddess of venom and breathing
epithets: She Who Causes the Throat to Breathe
entities.bio: Goddess of venomous stings, who both causes and cures them, and one of the four canopic guardians.
entities.longBio: Serqet's name means she who causes the throat to breathe, which reads either as a description of what she does for the healed or of the constriction she inflicts, and Egyptian religion is comfortable with both meanings at once: the power over venom is the power to withhold it. Her priests were practising physicians and magicians who treated scorpion stings, a serious hazard in a country where scorpions are common. She is one of the four goddesses - with Isis, Nephthys and Neith - who guard the canopic jars and the corners of the sarcophagus, and she watches over Qebehsenuef. She also appears among the goddesses who protect Isis and the infant Horus in the marshes, sending seven scorpions to accompany them.
entities.variantTraditions: Her scorpion is usually shown without its sting and claws, apparently to render the image safe to have nearby.

entities.name: Hapi
entities.role: God of the inundation
domains: the fertility of the black land
symbols: a heavy blue-green body with pendulous breasts
entities.abode: The caverns at the cataract from which the flood was believed to issue
entities.bio: The inundation personified: a well-fed figure with heavy breasts and a swollen belly, bringing abundance.
entities.longBio: Hapi is not the Nile itself but the flood - the annual rise that laid new silt across the fields and decided whether Egypt would eat. He is shown as a man with blue or green skin, a swollen belly and heavy breasts, because he nourishes, and the androgyny is deliberate rather than accidental. In scenes of the union of the Two Lands, two Hapi figures tie the papyrus and lotus together around the sema sign, binding Upper and Lower Egypt with the river that runs through both. He had no great temple, being honoured instead at the cataract and by offerings thrown into the water as the flood began, and hymns to him survive in numbers that reflect how much depended on him. His exact source was unknown and was said to lie in caverns guarded by Khnum.
entities.variantTraditions: Hapi shares his name with one of the four sons of Horus, who is a different figure entirely.

entities.name: Wepwawet
entities.role: Opener of the ways
domains: leading the dead into the underworld
symbols: the standing grey jackal or wolf
entities.bio: A jackal god who goes ahead: before the army, before the king, and before the dead.
entities.longBio: Wepwawet's name is a job description - opener of the ways - and it applies at every scale. His standard was carried in front of the king in procession and at the head of the army, clearing the road. In the funerary sphere he opens the way into the underworld for the dead, and his image presides over the Opening of the Mouth ceremony that restored the mummy's senses. At Abydos he led the great procession of Osiris. He is easily confused with Anubis, being also canine, but he is usually shown standing rather than couchant and coloured grey or white rather than black, and Greek visitors called his city Lycopolis, wolf-city, because they took him for a wolf.
entities.variantTraditions: Whether Wepwawet is a jackal or a wolf was already unclear in antiquity; the two were sometimes treated as one god with Anubis and sometimes kept separate.

entities.name: Sokar
entities.role: Falcon god of the Memphite necropolis
domains: the dark hours of the underworld
symbols: the falcon head on a mummiform body
festivals: The Festival of Sokar, with the henu barque dragged in procession
entities.bio: Hawk-headed lord of the Memphite cemetery and of the deepest hours of the night journey.
entities.longBio: Sokar governs the necropolis at Saqqara, which takes its name from him, and the region called Rosetau, understood as the entrance to the underworld passages. In the Book of the Underworld he presides over the fourth and fifth hours of the night, the darkest and most difficult stretch of the sun's journey, a sandy region the barque must be dragged through rather than sailed. He is a god of the dead but also, through his Memphite association with Ptah, a patron of metalworking. Fused into the composite Ptah-Sokar-Osiris, he appears in enormous numbers of small painted wooden statues placed in tombs of the Late Period. His festival involved dragging his henu barque, a boat mounted on a sledge, around the walls.
entities.variantTraditions: The three-part fusion Ptah-Sokar-Osiris merges creator, necropolis and resurrection into one funerary figure and is late; the three were originally distinct.

entities.name: Nefertum
entities.role: The lotus at the sun's first rising
epithets: The Lotus at the Nose of Ra
entities.bio: The blue lotus from which the sun first rose, and god of perfume.
entities.longBio: One creation account has the newborn sun rise from a blue lotus floating on the primeval waters, and Nefertum is that lotus. He completes the Memphite triad as the son of Ptah and Sekhmet, and is shown as a youth with a lotus blossom on his head, often flanked by two tall plumes. Because the blue lotus is intensely fragrant and opens at dawn to close at dusk, he is also the god of perfume and of the scented unguents Egyptians used heavily, and one text calls him the lotus at the nose of Ra - the flower the sun god holds to breathe. His character is gentle and his mother's is not, which is a pairing the Memphite theology seems to have found productive rather than contradictory.
entities.variantTraditions: In some accounts his mother is Bastet or Wadjet rather than Sekhmet, following whichever local goddess was Ptah's consort.

entities.name: Heqet
entities.role: Frog goddess of birth
entities.bio: Frog-headed midwife of the gods, who breathes life into the body Khnum has shaped.
entities.longBio: Egyptians watched the Nile fill with frogs as the inundation receded and read the animal as a sign of abundant new life, so the goddess of the last stage of birth is a frog. Heqet works alongside Khnum: he moulds the child on his wheel, and she gives it life and hastens the delivery. In the Westcar Papyrus she and a group of goddesses disguise themselves as travelling musicians to attend the birth of three future kings, which is one of the very few Egyptian narratives to show a birth in domestic detail. Amulets and wands carrying her image were used by women in labour, and her name appears on ivory knives meant to cut a protective circle around the birthing bed.
entities.variantTraditions: The much later Coptic association of the frog with resurrection may or may not descend from Heqet; the connection is asserted more often than demonstrated.

entities.name: Meskhenet
entities.role: Goddess of the birthing brick and of destiny
symbols: the birth brick with a human head
a headdress of two curled cow's uterus symbols
entities.abode: At the birthing bricks, and at the judgment
entities.bio: The brick Egyptian women squatted on to give birth, personified, who speaks each child's destiny.
entities.longBio: Egyptian women gave birth crouched on a pair of mud bricks, and Meskhenet is that brick made a goddess, shown either as a brick with a woman's head or as a woman wearing a curious two-pronged emblem. Her role goes beyond assisting: she declares the child's fate at the moment of birth, so that the shape of a life is spoken over it at the beginning. In the Westcar Papyrus she attends the births of the three kings and announces the kingship of each as it is born. She reappears at the other end of life, standing near the scales at the judgment, where she can testify to what the person was allotted - a neat closing of the circle, since the goddess who spoke the destiny is present when it is assessed.
entities.variantTraditions: Meskhenet is sometimes multiplied into four goddesses, one for each of the bricks or for each stage of the birth.

entities.name: Renenutet
entities.role: Cobra goddess of the harvest and of nursing
symbols: the cobra-headed woman nursing a child
entities.abode: The threshing floor and the granary
festivals: A harvest festival at the threshing floor, giving her name to the month Pharmuthi
entities.bio: The cobra of the harvest, who guards the granary and nurses the newborn.
entities.longBio: Snakes gathered in Egyptian granaries and threshing floors hunting rodents, and Renenutet is that observed fact turned into the goddess who protects the stored grain. Her festival fell at harvest, when offerings were made at the threshing floor, and her image guarded granaries and wine presses. Her second domain follows from the first: she nourishes, and so she suckles infants and is present at the giving of a name, which in Egyptian thought is part of what makes a person real. She is sometimes given as the mother of Nehebkau, and in a funerary context she can appear as the linen bandages that wrap the mummy. The month of Pharmuthi, and modern Coptic Parmoute, carries her name.
entities.variantTraditions: Her name is variously rendered Renenutet, Ernutet or Thermuthis; the Greeks identified her with Isis in her harvest aspect.

entities.name: Nehebkau
entities.role: Serpent who joins the ka to the body
domains: the binding of the ka to the body
symbols: a serpent with human arms and legs
entities.bio: A two-headed serpent who binds the ka to the body after death, making continued existence possible.
entities.longBio: Nehebkau begins as a hostile serpent of the underworld and is subdued - in one text Atum presses a fingernail to his spine - after which he becomes a servant of order rather than a threat. His name means he who harnesses or yokes the kas, and his function is precise and important: at death the ka, the vital essence, separates from the body, and Nehebkau reunites them so that the person can continue to exist. Without that joining the elaborate machinery of the tomb accomplishes nothing. He is also invoked against snakebite and scorpion venom, on the principle that the greatest serpent can restrain the lesser ones. In some texts he is a son of Renenutet, and in others he is counted among the assessors at the judgment.
entities.variantTraditions: His transformation from adversary to servant is not narrated so much as assumed; different texts treat him as either without reconciling them.

entities.name: The Four Sons of Horus
entities.role: Guardians of the organs of the dead
symbols: the four canopic jar stoppers: human, baboon, jackal and falcon
entities.abode: The canopic chest, beside the coffin
entities.bio: Four brothers who guard the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines, each with a goddess behind him.
entities.longBio: When a body was embalmed the liver, lungs, stomach and intestines were removed, dried, wrapped and placed in four jars, and each organ was assigned to one of the Four Sons of Horus, each of whom was in turn protected by one of the four goddesses. Imsety, human-headed, took the liver with Isis; Hapi, baboon-headed, the lungs with Nephthys; Duamutef, jackal-headed, the stomach with Neith; Qebehsenuef, falcon-headed, the intestines with Serqet. They are also aligned with the four cardinal points, which places the dead body at the centre of an ordered space. In earlier practice all four jar stoppers were human heads; the distinctive animal heads appear from the New Kingdom onward. The heart was deliberately left in the body, since it was needed for the weighing.
entities.variantTraditions: The Hapi of the canopic jars is a different god from Hapi of the inundation, sharing only the name.

entities.name: Aker
entities.role: The double lion of the horizon
domains: the horizon at both ends of the night
the guarding of the sun's passage
symbols: two lions or two human heads back to back
the strip of land between them
entities.abode: The eastern and western horizons at once
entities.bio: Two lions sitting back to back, the western and eastern gates the sun passes between each night.
entities.longBio: Aker is the earth understood as a passage rather than a surface. He is drawn as two lions seated back to back with the sun disc between them, or as a strip of land with a head at each end, and the two heads are named yesterday and tomorrow: the sun enters at the west, travels through the body of the earth all night, and leaves at the east. That makes him a doorway with a guard at both ends. He restrains the coils of Apep in the underworld and swallows the venom of anything that bites, and spells invoke him against snakes. The image of the double lion outlasted Egyptian religion, passing into later art as the pair of guardian lions flanking a gate.
entities.variantTraditions: Aker is sometimes pluralised into the Akeru, a group of earth-lions, and is closely related to Ruty, the double lion identified with Shu and Tefnut.

entities.name: Bata and Anpu
entities.role: The two brothers of the oldest surviving folk tale
entities.bio: Brothers of a Nineteenth Dynasty story: falsely accused, transformed repeatedly, and finally restored to the throne.
entities.longBio: The Tale of Two Brothers, on Papyrus D'Orbiney, is one of the oldest folk narratives to survive anywhere. Anpu's wife propositions his younger brother Bata; refused, she accuses him of assault, and Anpu waits with a knife. Warned by his cattle, Bata flees, proves his innocence by mutilating himself, and goes to the Valley of the Cedar, where he places his heart in a blossom at the top of a tree so that his life is stored outside his body. The gods make him a wife; she betrays him to the pharaoh and has the tree cut down, and Bata dies. Anpu searches years for the heart, finds it, and revives him. Bata then becomes a bull, is slaughtered; two persea trees spring from his blood, are cut down; a splinter enters his former wife's mouth and she bears him as her own son, who grows up to become king and to judge her.
entities.variantTraditions: The motif of the life hidden outside the body recurs across Eurasian folklore, and the opening episode has been compared with the Genesis account of Joseph and Potiphar's wife.

entities.name: Khufu
entities.role: The king of the Westcar Papyrus
entities.bio: Builder of the Great Pyramid, who in the Westcar Papyrus listens to his sons tell tales of magicians.
entities.longBio: Khufu is a historical Fourth Dynasty king, and almost nothing survives of him personally except the largest building of the ancient world and one tiny ivory statuette. What survives instead is a literary Khufu. The Westcar Papyrus frames a set of stories as entertainments told to a bored king by his sons: a wax crocodile that becomes a real one and takes an adulterer, a jewel retrieved from a lake by folding the water back, and the magician Djedi who can reattach a severed head and who prophesies that three kings not of Khufu's line will be born to the wife of a priest of Ra. Herodotus, writing two thousand years later, reports an Egyptian tradition that Khufu was a tyrant who closed the temples and forced the whole country to labour, a reputation that has no support in Egyptian sources.
entities.variantTraditions: Herodotus' hostile portrait is very late and probably reflects Late Period resentment of the pyramid age rather than any Old Kingdom memory.

entities.name: Djedi
entities.role: The magician of the Westcar Papyrus
entities.bio: A magician of a hundred and ten who reattaches severed heads and foretells the end of Khufu's line.
entities.longBio: Djedi is the last and most impressive of the magicians in the Westcar Papyrus, said to be a hundred and ten years old - the Egyptian ideal lifespan - and still eating five hundred loaves and drinking a hundred jugs of beer a day. Brought before Khufu, he is asked to demonstrate his reputed ability to reattach a severed head. A prisoner is offered; Djedi refuses flatly, saying it may not be done to a human being, and performs it instead on a goose, a waterbird and an ox. That refusal is the moral centre of the story and unusually explicit for Egyptian literature. He then delivers the prophecy Khufu actually wants: the secret chambers of Thoth will come to the eldest of three children about to be born to the wife of a priest of Ra, who will become kings after him.
entities.variantTraditions: The papyrus breaks off before the prophecy is fulfilled; the three children are presented as the first kings of the Fifth Dynasty.

entities.name: Sinuhe
entities.role: The exile who came home
entities.abode: Retjenu in the Levant, then Egypt
entities.bio: A court official who flees Egypt on the king's death, prospers abroad, and returns to be buried at home.
entities.longBio: The Story of Sinuhe is the most admired work of Egyptian literature and the one most often called a novel before novels. Overhearing news of Amenemhat I's assassination, Sinuhe panics for reasons the text never fully explains and flees, nearly dying of thirst before Bedouin rescue him. In Retjenu he marries a chief's daughter, becomes wealthy and powerful, and kills a champion who challenges him in single combat. Yet he cannot settle, because to die abroad is to be buried wrong, and the fear that grips him is not of death but of a foreign grave. Senusret I writes offering him return, and the reunion scene at court, where the royal children fail to recognise the sunburnt old man, is one of the finest things to survive from the ancient world. He is given a tomb, and the story ends with his shedding of the desert and reception of proper burial.
entities.variantTraditions: The historicity of Sinuhe is doubtful and largely beside the point; the text was copied for centuries as a model of fine writing.
